result:
The stranger on the 7:40 train looked up from her book and said, "Same weather's been doing this for three days," and I said, "Right? The sky looks like it's forgotten what it was supposed to do." And then we both laughed, and for four minutes — the whole route from Ashworth to Millpond — we talked about nothing at all. The kind of nothing that isn't actually nothing.

Here's the thing I've never been able to explain to anyone: a word is just a shape your mouth makes. *Sky.* The tongue resting against the roof, a soft k, the y gliding off like a cat's paw. And yet here it is, sitting between us, holding two people in the same small weather. Before we met, we were separate bodies on a train. Then I shaped a consonant and she shaped one back, and suddenly the distance between us wasn't three seats and a coat rack. It was a shared observation. A small, warm thing.

I think this is the whole thing, actually. We are all just mouths making shapes, hoping someone else's mouth will make a shape back, and that the shapes will land the same way in both of us. And most of the time, they do. And most of the time, we never need more than four minutes, a train, and the sky doing absolutely nothing.
